hints: Focus on what is different between the two experiments, the concentration of the acid, while everything else stays the same.
Reaction 2 uses 0.5 mol dm-3 acid compared to only 0.1 mol dm-3 in reaction 1, so think about which mixture has more crowded acid particles.
Link higher concentration to more frequent effective collisions per second, and then link that directly to a faster initial rate.
walkthrough:
**Compare the two conditions**

Think side by side. Both use the same mass of the same $\text{CuCO}_3$ powder and the acid is in excess in both.

The only change is $[\text{HNO}_3]$: $0.1 \, \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ in reaction 1 versus $0.5 \, \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ in reaction 2.

**Apply collision theory to initial rate**

Higher concentration means more $\text{H}^+$ ions per unit volume, so more frequent collisions with the $\text{CuCO}_3$ surface.

$$\text{CuCO}_3(\text{s}) + 2\text{HNO}_3(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{Cu(NO}_3)_2(\text{aq}) + \text{CO}_2(\text{g}) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l})$$

So reaction 2 starts faster than reaction 1.

**Work out both ratios**

Since rate 1 is smaller than rate 2:
$$\frac{\text{rate of reaction 1}}{\text{rate of reaction 2}} < 1$$

Rate is proportional to the number of effective collisions per second, so reaction 1 also has fewer effective collisions per second than reaction 2:
$$\frac{\text{initial effective collisions in 1 per second}}{\text{initial effective collisions in 2 per second}} < 1$$

Both ratios are less than 1.

options.A: Incorrect. This says both ratios are greater than 1, meaning reaction 1 is faster. That is backwards, the more dilute 0.1 mol dm-3 acid cannot give a faster rate or more collisions per second than the 0.5 mol dm-3 acid.
options.B: Incorrect. The second ratio is correct as less than 1, but the first ratio is wrong. If reaction 1 has fewer effective collisions per second, it must also have the slower rate, so rate 1 / rate 2 cannot be greater than 1.
options.C: Incorrect. The first ratio is correct as less than 1, but the second ratio is wrong. Rate and frequency of effective collisions go together, so you cannot have a slower rate but more effective collisions per second in reaction 1.
options.D: Correct. Reaction 2 has the higher acid concentration, so it has more effective collisions per second and a faster initial rate of $\text{CO}_2$ production. Therefore both rate 1 / rate 2 and collisions 1 / collisions 2 are less than 1.
